entry: Non-penetrative sex act, performed as [[Foreplay|foreplay]] or as an alternative to penetrative sex. A man's penis is placed between a woman's breasts and stimulated by thrusting or rubbing; lubricant or saliva may be used, and the act may be combined with [[Oral sex|oral sex]]. Because it is non-penetrative, the risk of passing a [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infection]] that requires contact with semen or pre-ejaculate, such as [[HIV]], is greatly reduced. The act is common in [[Pornography|pornography]]. [[Sigmund Freud]] considered such extensions of sexual interest to fall within the normal range unless marked by exclusivity.

Indian actor and film producer, known mainly for [[Malayalam]]-language films. He has appeared in more than 400 films over a career of more than five decades, mostly in lead roles, across Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, [[Kannada]], [[Hindi]], and [[English language|English]] cinema. The [[Government of India]] awarded him the Padma Shri, the fourth-highest civilian award, in 1998. He is chairman of Malayalam Communications, which runs the Kairali TV channels, and owns the production company Mammootty Kampany.

Extinct elephantid genus, *Mammuthus*, related to modern [[Elephant|elephants]]. Mammoths lived from the late [[Miocene]] (around 6.2 million years ago) into the [[Holocene]] and inhabited Africa, Asia, Europe, and North America at various times. They are distinguished from living elephants by spirally twisted tusks and, in some later species, a thick coat of fur. The oldest species, *Mammuthus subplanifrons*, appeared in southern and eastern Africa around 6 million years ago. The [[Woolly mammoth]] (*M. primigenius*) evolved 700–400,000 years ago in [[Siberia]], and survived on Wrangel Island in the [[Arctic Ocean]] until about 4,000 years ago. Mammoths and [[Asian elephant|Asian elephants]] are more closely related to each other than either is to African elephants. In 1796 the French biologist [[Georges Cuvier]] first identified woolly mammoth remains as an extinct species.

American-born, French-naturalized visual artist who spent most of his career in [[Paris]]. Born Emmanuel Radnitzky in South [[Philadelphia]] to Russian Jewish immigrants, he adopted the name Man Ray. He contributed to the [[Dada]] and [[Surrealism|Surrealist]] movements, although his ties to each were informal, and considered himself a painter above all. He is best known for photograms he called *rayographs*, after himself, made by placing objects directly on photosensitive paper and exposing them to light. He also worked as a fashion and portrait photographer and made films and readymades, such as *Cadeau* (1921), an iron fitted with tacks. Items linked to his father's tailoring trade, such as [[Sewing machine|sewing machines]] and mannequins, appear throughout his work. In Paris he was associated with [[Tristan Tzara]].

City (pop., 2023: 1,063,815), capital and largest city of [[Nicaragua]], on the shore of Lake Managua. It is one of the largest cities in [[Central America]] and the seat of Managua Department. The area was inhabited by [[Paleo-Indians]] as far back as 12,000 BC. Founded in 1819, Managua became the national capital in 1852, having been a small fishing village before then. Between 1842 and 1930 it grew rapidly and became one of the most developed cities in Central America. A 1931 earthquake killed between 1,000 and 2,450 people, and the 1972 earthquake destroyed 90% of the downtown and killed more than 19,120 people. The city has been rebuilt several times and remains a major economic hub for the country and Central America.

Genus of large, fully aquatic, mostly herbivorous marine mammals, also called sea cows. Three living species, members of the order [[Sirenia]], inhabit shallow, marshy coastal areas and rivers of the [[Caribbean Sea]], the [[Gulf of Mexico]], the Amazon basin, and [[West Africa]]. They eat more than 60 freshwater and saltwater plants and can grow up to 4.0 m (13 ft 1 in) long. Human activity is the main cause of death, through habitat destruction and collisions with propeller-driven boats; some have been found with over 50 propeller scars.

City (pop., 2024: 2,279,686), capital of the Brazilian state of Amazonas, near the confluence of the [[Rio Negro (Amazon)|Negro]] and [[Amazon River|Amazon]] rivers. It is Brazil's seventh-largest city and one of two cities in the [[Amazon rainforest]] with more than 1 million people, alongside [[Belém]]. The Portuguese built the Fort of São José do Rio Negro there in 1669, and the settlement was named Manaus in 1832. Rubber made it the richest city in South America in the late 1800s and earned it the nickname Paris of the Tropics. Its economy centers on the Industrial Park of Manaus, a free economic zone whose factories make electronics, chemical products, and soap. The city was one of 12 Brazilian host cities for the 2014 World Cup.

Family of two-player count-and-capture [[Board game|board games]] played with seeds, stones, or beans in rows of pits. A turn consists of taking all the seeds from one pit and sowing them one per pit in sequence. A player who ends a turn in an empty pit on their own side captures the opponent's seeds in the pit directly across. The word derives from the Arabic root *naqala*, meaning to move. Its origins are disputed. Claimed boards from Jordan date to about 5,870 BC, a claim others dispute, while excavated boards and rock cuts in Eritrea and Ethiopia date to the 6th and 7th centuries AD. The game reached the Americas through the [[Atlantic slave trade]], and the traditional game Warra was still played in [[Louisiana]] in the early 20th century.

City (pop., 2024: over 589,000) and metropolitan borough in North West [[England]]. It forms the core of the Greater Manchester Built-up Area, which has 2.87 million people and is one of the most populous conurbations in the [[United Kingdom]]. The city's history began with a civilian settlement associated with a Roman fort, Mamucium, established around AD 79 near the confluence of the Medlock and Irwell rivers. Manchester became the world's first industrialized city during the [[Industrial Revolution]], driven by textile manufacture, and gained city status in 1853. The Manchester Ship Canal, opened in 1894, linked the city to the [[Irish Sea]], 36 miles (58 km) west. Deindustrialization after the Second World War reduced its fortunes, and extensive regeneration followed the 1996 bombing. Manchester hosted the 2002 Commonwealth Games. It is noted for its architecture, music, media, and sports clubs.

City (pop., 2020: 115,644), largest city in [[New Hampshire]], United States, on the banks of the Merrimack River. It is the tenth-most populous city in [[New England]] and, with Nashua, is one of two seats of Hillsborough County. Samuel Blodget is credited with the name, reflecting his hope of building an industrial center like the English city of [[Manchester]]. During the [[Industrial Revolution]], the Amoskeag Manufacturing Company operated the largest cotton textile plant in the world. Many textile jobs left after [[World War II]], but new industries, including DEKA, arrived.

[[Association football]] club in the [[Premier League]], based at Old Trafford, Greater Manchester, England. Founded in 1878 as Newton Heath LYR Football Club and renamed in 1902, it is nicknamed the Red Devils. Under [[Alex Ferguson]], manager from 1986 to 2013, the club won 13 league titles and two [[UEFA Champions League]] titles, and in 1998–99 became the first English club to win the continental treble. Its 20 top-flight league titles are a joint record. The Glazer family has controlled the club since Malcolm Glazer's 2005 purchase, and some shares have been listed on the New York Stock Exchange since 2012.

Tungusic ethnic group native to [[Manchuria]] in Northeast Asia, the people from whom the region takes its name. The Manchus are descended from the Jurchen people who founded the [[Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|Jin dynasty]], a claim disputed by historians. They established the Later Jin (1616–1636) and [[Qing dynasty]] (1636–1912) dynasties of China. In 1635 Hong Taiji adopted Manchu as the official name, replacing Jurchen. About half of the Manchu population lives in Liaoning and one-fifth in [[Hebei]].

Japanese puppet state in [[Manchuria]] (1932–1945). Established by the [[Empire of Japan]] after its invasion of Manchuria in 1931 following the Mukden incident, it received limited diplomatic recognition, mainly from states aligned with the [[Axis powers]], and its existence is widely regarded as illegitimate. Its nominal head was [[Puyi]], the final emperor of China, but Japanese officials made the decisions. More than one million Japanese settled in the state by 1945, and heavy industry expanded using forced labor. Manchukuo was the launching ground for Japan's invasion of China in the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]]. The Soviet invasion of Manchuria in August 1945 ended it.

Historical region in Northeast Asia, encompassing present-day [[China|Northeast China]] and parts of the Russian Far East. In a narrow sense it comprises the Chinese provinces of Heilongjiang, Jilin, and Liaoning, along with parts of Hebei and Inner Mongolia. In a broader sense it includes the [[Amur|Amur River]] basin, parts of which the [[Qing dynasty]] ceded to the [[Russian Empire]] in the Amur Annexation of 1858–1860. The region is home to the [[Manchu people|Manchus]], Mongols, Koreans, Nanai, Nivkhs, and Ulchs, and was the ancestral homeland of the Jurchens. The name is an exonym of Japanese origin, and the [[Empire of Japan]] promoted it to support its puppet state, [[Manchukuo]]. Chinese usage now avoids the term, and the area is commonly called the Northeast.

City (pop., 2014: 1,225,553), second-largest city in [[Myanmar]], on the east bank of the [[Irrawaddy River]], 631 km north of [[Yangon]]. King Mindon founded it in 1857 to replace Amarapura as the royal capital of the [[Konbaung dynasty]]. It was the last royal capital before the kingdom's annexation by the [[British Empire]] in 1885, after which the British shifted commercial and political importance to Yangon. Extensive destruction occurred during the Japanese conquest of Burma in the Second World War. The city became part of the independent Union of Burma in 1948. It remains the economic center of Upper Myanmar and is considered the center of Burmese culture. Since the late 20th century, an influx of Chinese immigrants, mostly from [[Yunnan]], has reshaped its ethnic makeup.

Largest branch of the Sinitic languages, natively spoken by 71% of Chinese speakers, with nearly one billion speakers as a group. Its varieties stretch from [[Yunnan]] in the southwest to [[Xinjiang]] in the northwest and Heilongjiang in the northeast. Most varieties have four lexical tones, and many retain retroflex initial consonants. Some form of Mandarin served as a lingua franca for officials and courts from at least the 14th century. In the early 20th century a standard based on the Beijing dialect was adopted as the national language. Standard Chinese is the official language of [[China]] and [[Taiwan]], one of four official languages of [[Singapore]], and one of six official languages of the [[United Nations]]. It is the most commonly taught form of Chinese as a foreign language.

Small, rounded [[Citrus]] fruit, *Citrus reticulata*, usually eaten fresh or in fruit salads. The mandarin is oblate, unlike the roughly spherical sweet orange, which is a mandarin-pomelo hybrid. Its thin, loose peel makes it easier to peel and split into segments than most citrus. Ripe fruit is firm to slightly soft, heavy for its size, and pebbly-skinned. The tree is easily damaged by cold and grows in tropical and subtropical areas. Genetic studies indicate that the wild mandarin was one of the original citrus species and is an ancestor of many hybrids. Most commercial strains derive from hybridization with [[Pomelo|pomelo]], which gives them sweet fruit; the ancestral mandarin was bitter. The wild mandarin evolved in a restricted region of South China and [[Vietnam]].

Chinese political doctrine of divine legitimacy for rulers, used in ancient and imperial [[China]]. Heaven was held to bestow its mandate on a virtuous ruler, the Son of Heaven, and to withdraw it if the ruler proved unworthy. Famine and flood were read as signs of Heaven's displeasure, and revolts often followed major disasters. The mandate did not require noble birth; dynasties such as the Han and Ming were founded by men of common origin but were seen as having succeeded because they gained it. The doctrine implied a right of rebellion against an unjust ruler. The classical statement of that right, in [[Mencius]], was often edited out of the text. The [[Zhou dynasty]] first used the concept to justify overthrowing the [[Shang dynasty]], and later dynasties, including the [[Qing dynasty]], invoked it.

British-administered [[League of Nations]] mandate territory (1920–1948). Britain administered it from 1922 under the Mandate for Palestine, after British forces drove the [[Ottoman Empire]] out of the Levant in 1917–18 during [[World War I]]. The [[Balfour Declaration]] of 1917 promised support for a Jewish "national home"; critics argue that it overrode self-determination for the Palestinian Arab population. Immigration and rising nationalism led to the 1936–1939 Arab revolt and a 1944–1948 Jewish insurgency. In 1947 the [[United Nations]] proposed partition. After the 1948 war the territory was divided among [[Israel]], Transjordan, and Egypt, which established an "All-Palestine Protectorate" in the [[Gaza Strip]].

[[Fractal]] in the complex plane, named after mathematician [[Benoit Mandelbrot]]. It is the set of complex numbers *c* for which the iteration *z* → *z*² + *c*, starting at *z* = 0, remains bounded. Robert W. Brooks and Peter Matelski first defined and drew it in 1978, and in 1980 Mandelbrot produced high-quality images at [[IBM]]'s research center in Yorktown Heights, New York. Its boundary is a fractal curve showing ever finer detail at higher magnifications, and it is widely cited as an example of mathematical beauty.

Small plucked [[String instrument|stringed instrument]] in the [[Lute|lute]] family, usually with eight strings in four courses tuned in perfect fifths, like a [[Violin|violin]] (G3, D4, A4, E5). Mandolins evolved from European lutes, and the Neapolitan mandolin emerged in [[Italy]]. The three main styles are the round-backed Neapolitan, the archtop, and the flat-backed mandolin. Neapolitan mandolins feature prominently in European classical music, including the works of [[Antonio Vivaldi]]. Archtop instruments are common in American folk, old-time, and bluegrass music, and flat-backed ones in Irish, British, and Brazilian folk music. Metal strings, which exert more pressure than gut, led to the stronger soundboards of modern instruments.

Large [[Old World monkey]] of west central Africa, one of the most colorful mammals, with red and blue skin on its face and rump. Males are larger, with longer canines and brighter coloring. Mandrills mainly live in [[Tropical rainforest|tropical rainforests]], forage on the ground for fruit and seeds, and form hordes that can number in the hundreds, with females at the core of each group. The species is classified as vulnerable by the IUCN, which cites habitat destruction and bushmeat hunting as its main threats. [[Gabon]] is considered its stronghold.

Large [[Canidae|canid]] of South America, neither a fox nor a wolf despite its foxlike markings. It weighs 20–30 kg and stands up to 110 cm at the withers. The solitary, crepuscular omnivore helps disperse fruits such as the wolf apple (*Solanum lycocarpum*). It lives in open grassland and savanna in [[Brazil]], [[Paraguay]], [[Argentina]], and [[Bolivia]]. The IUCN lists it as near threatened. In 2011 a female hit by a truck received [[Stem cell|stem cell]] treatment at the Zoo Brasília, the first recorded use of stem cells to heal injuries in a wild animal.

German [[World War I]] fighter pilot, known as the Red Baron. Born near [[Wrocław]] (then Breslau) into the [[Prussia|Prussian]] nobility, he was a *Freiherr*, usually translated as baron. A former cavalryman, he transferred to the air service in 1915 and led the fighter unit Jasta 11 in 1917 before commanding Jagdgeschwader I, known as the Flying Circus. Credited with 80 air combat victories, the highest total of the war, he painted his aircraft red, which gave rise to his nickname. He was shot down and killed near Vaux-sur-Somme, France, and the circumstances of his death have been widely debated.

Comics or graphic novels originating in [[Japan]]. Manga are typically printed in black and white, serialized in large anthology magazines, and collected in *tankōbon* volumes. Genres range from action, romance, and horror to [[Science fiction|science fiction]] and fantasy. Manga has been a major part of Japan's publishing industry since the 1950s. The Japanese market was valued at ¥586.4 billion in 1995 and reached a record ¥704.3 billion in 2024, with digital manga accounting for about ¥500 billion. In 2021 manga made up 76% of US comics and graphic novel sales, according to NPD BookScan. Pioneers such as [[Osamu Tezuka]] refined cinematic storytelling in the 1950s and 1960s. Related comics in other languages include manhua in Chinese and manhwa in Korean.
